Selectable text over a raster page

A page image says what the document looks like. It says nothing a reader can select, a search box can find, or a screen reader can speak. The text layer is the other half.

Every run in this document was placed from SnapDOM’s final artifact DOM, measured with getClientRects(), and written under render mode 3 Tr so the glyphs paint nothing at all. What you see is the raster underneath; what you copy is this. The two agree because both come from the same final serialized layout, mounted in the same frame — and the sweep in verify.mjs is what turns that sentence into a number.

Why word granularity

A line-level run leans on the substitute font’s own advance widths to space the characters inside it, so the highlight drifts away from the pixels a few words in and never comes back. Per word the drift is bounded by the word: each one gets its own Tm and its own horizontal scale, and the error cannot accumulate across the line. It costs more operators. It buys a selection that lands where the reader is looking.

“We kept asking why the highlight slid to the right on long lines, and the answer was that nobody had ever pinned the advance to anything the browser measured.”

The horizontal scale is the correction. Chromium reports the advance the real font produced, including letter spacing, word spacing and every shaping decision; the base-14 substitute produces a different one; and Tz is the ratio between them, clamped so a degenerate measurement cannot stretch a run to a thousand percent. Set it wrong and the run is still on the right line, still starting in the right place, and still visibly the wrong width when you drag across it.

What the sweep actually asserts

A compound such as text-layer-geometry-notes breaks at its own hyphens, and each piece is a client rect of its own.

For each word: the origin the content stream carries, against the left edge of the box the browser reported for that same word. For each word again: the painted advance, reconstructed from Tz and the substitute’s own metrics, against the width of that box. Both in points, both relative to the element’s border box, with no fitting, no averaging and no per-page fudge factor.

Origin
The baseline start point. Untransformed it is the left edge of the client rect, and the top edge plus the ascent — a number the browser lays out from the font’s own metrics and the layer reads with a zero-height inline baseline probe in the artifact’s own document.
Advance
The distance the text cursor travels. It is the one quantity the raster and the layer can disagree about while both look correct in isolation.
Matrix
Null when nothing rotates, so the common path stays exactly as cheap as it was before rotation existed at all.

Six probes pin six words and prove the mechanism. Hundreds of words prove the absence of the case nobody thought of: the italic that shifts by a hairline, the inline code span whose monospace substitute is a different width, the capitalised heading whose transform never reached the text node, the small emphatic label that is tracked out by a pixel per character. None of those is a probe anyone would have written. All of them are in here, and all of them are counted.

DRAFT REVIEW

The parts that are not covered here

Text outside WinAnsi goes out through a Type0 font and is addressed by glyph identifier rather than by byte, so a byte comparison cannot read it back; the unicode fixture owns that path. Form control values carry no text node and no client rect, so they are placed from layout metrics instead; forms owns those. Shadow roots, overflow clipping and opacity each have a fixture of their own. This one is deliberately made of nothing but ORDINARY VISIBLE PROSE, because its claim is about quantity: not that a hard case works, but that the easy case works everywhere, several hundred times in a row, with no exception the file forgot to mention.

Read the artifacts as well as the numbers. The debug render paints this layer in red instead of in nothing, and a text layer sliding off its raster is a thing you see in a quarter of a second and argue about for an hour. See the text layer notes and the pagination notes for the rest, and remember that an escape such as \n or a call such as toPdf(element, options) has to survive the PDF string escaping on its way in… which is the sort of thing a sweep notices and a probe does not.
